# Rifled firearms (rifling, Minié ball, breech-loader) (`rifling_minie_breechloader`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs handguns_muskets; helped by lathe_screw_cutting, interchangeable_parts, ballistics_gunnery
- Core idea: Spiral grooves cut inside the barrel grip the bullet and spin it, and a spinning bullet flies point-first without swerving, so accuracy rises from about 80 m to several hundred. The old difficulty was loading: a bullet tight enough to take the grooves had to be hammered down the muzzle. The Minié bullet is a pointed lead cylinder with a hollow base, dropped in loose and swelled into the grooves by the gas. Loading at the breech with a cartridge that carries bullet, powder and primer together then lets a man fire lying down, several times faster.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking the spin adds force; it only stabilises
  - A breech that leaks hot gas into the firer's face; the seal was solved by the expanding brass cartridge case
  - Black powder fouling clogs grooves within a few dozen shots
  - A slow rifle bullet drops steeply, so range must be judged well; much of the theoretical gain was lost in battle
  - Cutting uniform grooves needs a rifling bench with a guide; it cannot be filed by hand
- History: europe: c. 1500 – rifled barrels in south Germany and Austria (the names and dates usually given for an inventor are legend); 18th c. – hunting and Jäger rifles; 1742 – Robins explains why spin steadies the ball; 1777 – Ferguson breech-loading rifles in British service; 1841 – Prussia adopts the Dreyse needle gun; 1849 – Minié bullet; 1860s – metallic cartridges; americas: 18th c. – Pennsylvania long rifle; 1861–1865 – rifle muskets general in the Civil War; east_asia: 1860s – Japan imports Minié and breech-loading rifles in the Boshin War era
- Read:
  - Benjamin Robins, New Principles of Gunnery (1742)
  - Earl J. Hess, The Rifle Musket in Civil War Combat: Reality and Myth (2008)
